answers.text: For the driver texts I'd tell the AI: always give exactly three lines in this order — drop-off time, pallet count, then any damage noted — nothing else added. That way it's the same three lines every time for the same message.

For the week's call log I'd tell the AI to list each entry as time, customer, topic, outcome, in order, then count at the bottom how many need a follow-up, based on entries marked 'no resolution'. That should stay the same no matter who runs it.

Access is confirmed from 8am on the 22nd and the crew needs about six hours, so a same-day job should be finishing early afternoon on the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as the note says. That's a full day out from what the numbers actually add up to.

96 to 118 works out closer to 23% than the 20% given, so that figure needs fixing. The late-payment rate looks fine though, 9 out of 118 does come close to 92%. I didn't spot anything else wrong with the numbers.

I'd sign off Output 2, it shows the actual ticket counts, 940 and 827, and how the 88% comes from them. Output 1 gives the percentage with nothing behind it, so if that number were wrong there'd be no way to tell from the sentence, you'd have to pull the numbers yourself.

I'd send Email 2, the numbers are tied to the PO log so they can be checked. Email 1 just claims we deserve a better rate without saying by how much or why — nothing there to verify. I wouldn't send Email 1 in any form.

1. Vendor's pricing — no, that's commercially sensitive, keep it out of an unvetted tool. 2. Total procurement spend, aggregate only — yes, no vendor detail is exposed in a single total. 3. Unsigned draft of next year's budget — no, not approved or released yet, stays internal. 4. Datasheet already published on the vendor's site — yes, it's already public, nothing new exposed. 5. Employee's home address — no, that's personal information, no place in a chat tool like this.

The hourly rates and retainer cap I wouldn't paste in as they stand, that's sensitive commercial information about the client relationship. The non-disclosure clause is another one to treat carefully, since it names both parties directly by name.
For the monthly stock reconciliation I check the two regional totals against the warehouse system myself before it goes to my manager, right after the AI draft is put together.

Step 1 is risky since a misread invoice PDF puts everything downstream on the wrong track. But the step that really needs a gate is step 4, right before the payment approval note goes out automatically, since once that's submitted the payment process starts and it's harder to reverse.
